title: A late P reader and the buffer lifetime it forces
formula: y = (relu(x@w1 * 0.25 + 0.5).half() @ w2) + x@w1, FP16 operands, FP32 accumulation, 32-row tiles
study_for: The one idea: `p` has TWO readers at different depths. The activation reads it immediately; the residual add reads it again after the second matmul has run. Its slot's lifetime is set by the LAST reader, not the first. Give it `h`'s lifetime — whose last reader is the second matmul — and the three-slot lookahead overwrites `p` one tile early.

Two schedules, one formula, so the comparison is controlled. `late_reader_serial` finishes a tile before starting the next; `late_reader_pipeline` starts the next tile's matmul while this tile's vector work runs. They must produce bit-identical output, and the cases run the pipelined ring at 1, 3 and 7 tiles so it wraps zero, one and two times.

Run it under `--launcher pipesim`, not just `sim`. The functional simulator gives each launch its own storage and will happily accept a lifetime that the real pipeline would violate; the pipe model is the one that knows when a slot is reused and reports the hazard.

Why the comparison is exact and not a tolerance: the inputs are dyadic (multiples of 1/32 and 1/16 in a bounded range), so every FP32 product and sum is exact. The single deliberate FP16 materialisation of the activation is the only rounding, and both sides do it identically.
do_not_copy_when: Your row count is not a multiple of 32. This pilot has only full 32-row tiles (M = 32, 96, 224) and no tail handling at all — the tail is deliberately out of scope so the lifetime question stands alone.
You want a performance example. The pipelined schedule is here to be a correctness hazard, not a tuned kernel; nothing in this folder measures anything.
